policies.name: Two gates
policies.desc: Gate 1 decides whether an artifact EXISTS for a viewer (component 13, audience). Gate 2 decides which ROWS a viewer sees inside it (component 12, data scope). They are independent: a viewer can be correctly entitled and correctly see zero rows.

policies.name: Counts are computed
policies.desc: Every count on this screen — "sees 8 of 60" — is derived from the roster at paint time. No count is stored. A stated count stops being true the moment the roster changes and nothing notices.

policies.name: Rule shape
policies.desc: A person is full-scope, or restricted by exactly one BASIS field plus the values of it they may see. A separate boolean mask hides row-level money while leaving totals visible.

policies.name: Legal basis
policies.desc: A field qualifies as a restriction basis only if every one of its values maps to a definite, non-empty set of the roster. Continuous measures — forecast, EAC variance, percent complete — are excluded: a rule on them re-resolves every week, which makes it a filter, not an access rule.

policies.name: No approval
policies.desc: There is no approval queue. Publishing, granting and revoking are immediate and logged. (Superseded the earlier CAPEX draft, which carried a six-item approval queue.)

policies.name: Admin holds none
policies.desc: The platform administrator administers entitlement and does not thereby acquire it. Their zero scope is by design, not omission.

policies.name: Publishing never widens
policies.desc: Adding a reader to an artifact grants existence, never rows. The reader opens it under their own rule.

review_items.title: 'Working Forecast' proposed as a Plan Vintage member - create the node?
review_items.detail: epbcs.version carries Working alongside MTP2026_v3 and 3+9, so the profiler nominated it as a fourth vintage. It is not one. Working is a selector that resolves to whichever produced round is latest. Accepting it would let a query pin vintage=Working and get an answer whose meaning changes the day the next round is cut, with no version of the question having changed.
evidence: 6+6 and 9+3 are structurally zero - rounds not produced

review_items.title: Grantham Materials Laboratory, LLC - same firm across 3 projects, merge to one vendor?
review_items.detail: The firm is named in the party block of contracts filed under different projects. Both sides of the match were read out of a document, which makes this the lowest-confidence merge class in the graph. Approving it is what makes vendor concentration answerable at portfolio level; getting it wrong attributes one firm's exposure to another.
evidence: src_drive contract entity confidence 0.86 - lowest in the graph

review_items.title: Change order rider -> contract, matched on a contract number printed in the PDF
review_items.detail: 22 change orders were tied to their contracts by the contract number on the rider's face. Every AMENDS edge in the graph is extracted. A wrong match moves a priced amendment onto the wrong contract, which moves it onto the wrong project and the wrong vendor - three wrong answers from one bad join.

review_items.title: Caleb Kaltmeier and Dorothea Kaltmeier - merge on surname?
review_items.detail: The manager column carries two naming conventions and the normaliser handles the format. A surname collision is not an identity signal and the rule does not act on one. This sits in the queue as a declined match rather than being silently dropped, so a reviewer can see where the line is drawn.
evidence: format normalisation applies; surname-only matching does not

review_items.title: Authorized Amount resolved from the plan version chain (DR-5)
review_items.detail: There is no authorised-amount column. It is derived by taking the most recent approval date in northline_psoft.appr. On 2,426 projects the Most Recent Budget Plan and the Active Budget Plan disagree, so the rule decides which number the word 'authorised' means. The rule itself is still open (DR-5) and this queue item is where it gets settled.
evidence: 2,426 projects where Most Recent != Active Budget Plan
ds_psoft_appr is the connector's freshness floor - 7 days behind

review_items.title: Two BU codes aliasing one display label (DR-6)
review_items.detail: The entity-mapping upload carries an alias column in which more than one BU code can resolve to the same display label. Merging the codes would make BU rollups add up and make ownership unanswerable. They stay separate with the label aliased.

review_items.title: 'No State' nominated as a State - create the node?
review_items.detail: Every Shared Services Division row carries the literal string No State in attributes.state. The profiler saw a fifth distinct value and nominated it. It is a sentinel, not a place. Accepting it would hang a rate jurisdiction off something that has no commission and would quietly fold overheads into every spend-by-state answer.
evidence: attributes.state distinct values: Ardenia, Belmara, Corvale, Dunmoor, 'No State'
all 'No State' rows belong to Shared Services Division

pivot.title: 'Working Forecast' proposed as a Plan Vintage member - create the node?
pivot.detail: epbcs.version carries Working alongside MTP2026_v3 and 3+9, so the profiler nominated it as a fourth vintage. It is not one. Working is a selector that resolves to whichever produced round is latest. Accepting it would let a query pin vintage=Working and get an answer whose meaning changes the day the next round is cut, with no version of the question having changed.
pivot.why_pivot: This item changes what a word means, not what a row says. Accepting it silently would change the meaning of every answer that names it.
evidence: 6+6 and 9+3 are structurally zero - rounds not produced

sanity_checks.question: Which projects are forecasting above their approved plan, and by how much?
sanity_checks.verdict: Answerable - with a declared materiality floor
sanity_checks.verdict_body: The walk is Project -> MEAS:total_budget_working and Project -> MEAS:most_recent_budget_plan, differenced per project. It is answerable only with a floor stated on the face of the answer: 3,688 of 4,500 projects show a positive gap, so an unfiltered ranking is noise. At the declared floor - gap >= $2m AND >= 5% of plan - 2,966 projects qualify.
sanity_checks.plan:
MATCH (p:Project)-[:AGGREGATES_OVER]-(m:Measure)
WHERE m.id IN ['MEAS:total_budget_working','MEAS:most_recent_budget_plan']
RETURN p, gap = working - plan ORDER BY gap DESC

sanity_checks.question: What is our exposure to any single contractor across the portfolio?
sanity_checks.verdict: Answerable for the contract corpus only
sanity_checks.verdict_body: Vendor -> Contract -> Project resolves cleanly, but the corpus is 31 contracts across 5 projects. The honest answer names the vendor concentration inside that corpus and states that the other 4,495 projects have no contract documents in scope. Presenting it as portfolio exposure would be wrong.

sanity_checks.question: Which projects hold an authorization but show no activity this year?
sanity_checks.verdict: Declined as asked - no natural instances
sanity_checks.verdict_body: Taken literally the question returns zero rows: projects In Planning carry both zero actuals and zero calendarized budget, so 'holds an authorization' and 'no activity' never co-occur in this extract. The answerable form is 'no FY26 actuals against a non-zero Active Budget Plan', and the answer must say it was relaxed.
sanity_checks.plan: MATCH (p:Project) WHERE p.active_budget_plan > 0 AND p.fy26_actuals = 0 RETURN p

ask_answers.question: Are we going to spend the authorized capital this fiscal year?
ask_answers.summary: No. The Working Forecast lands FY26 at $11.39b against a $12.03b working budget — $639.7m short.

blocks.markdown:
Read against the **Working Forecast** — the live, continuously-updated cut, not a forecast round — FY26 lands at **$11,388,920,975** against a working budget of **$12,028,661,826**. That is an underspend of **$639,740,851**, or 5.3% of the year.

The **3+9 forecast round** — the only formal round that ran this year — says **$12,021,894,758**, essentially on budget. The two disagree by **$632,973,783** because the 3+9 was cut in March and the working forecast has absorbed two months of actuals since. Which number you quote depends on whether you are reporting to a forecast round or to today.

ask_answers.question: Where is authorized capital stalling — which stage of the chain is it stuck at?
ask_answers.summary: The chain breaks at commitment. Authorization is $113.08b, actuals are $24.01b, and the commitment stage between them is not in the connected data.

blocks.markdown:
The capital chain runs **Budget → Authorization → Commitment → Actual → CWIP → Capitalized**. Two of those six stages are present in the connected sources.

Authorization is **$113,075,048,000** across 4,500 projects (Active Budget Plan, `northline_epbcs.plan`). Actual cost inception-to-date is **$24,010,050,019** (`northline_psoft.gl`). Between them sits the commitment stage — purchase orders and contract obligations — and **there is no connected source for it**. `northline_psoft.appr` carries approval workflow, not commitment value.

So the honest answer is that 21.2% of authorized capital has reached actuals, and the remaining 78.8% is either committed or uncommitted — and this data cannot tell you which.

blocks.title: Capital chain — value present at each stage
blocks.note: Commitment, CWIP and Capitalized read zero because no source is connected for them. That is an absence of data, not a balance of zero.

blocks.markdown: **What to connect.** A commitment source — the PeopleSoft purchasing module or the contract register — would close the largest gap. A fixed-asset ledger feed would close CWIP and Capitalized. Until then, questions from HQ-20 through HQ-27 either decline or answer against a proxy, and the proxy is named every time.

evidence.detail: Active Budget Plan, Total Budget (Working)
ITD Actuals
No commitment, CWIP or capitalization source in the connected set

ask_answers.question: How much of this year's plan is uncommitted with a quarter to go?
ask_answers.summary: Cannot answer — no commitment source is connected.

blocks.markdown:
This needs contracted commitment (K-07), and there is no source for it in the connected set. The four BigQuery datasets carry plan, general-ledger actuals, approval workflow and project attributes; none of them carries purchase-order or contract-obligation value.

**Uncommitted is not the same as unspent.** I can tell you that **$7,622,994,230** of the FY26 working budget is unspent as of 2026-05-31 (FY26 actuals close at May). I cannot tell you how much of that is already under contract, and reporting the unspent figure as though it were the uncommitted figure would overstate your procurement runway by whatever is already committed.

There is a related figure in the data — 207 budget lines flagged **Unencumbered**, carrying $10,477,911,371. That flag sits at business unit × budget category grain, not project grain, and it is a plan attribute rather than a commitment reading. It answers a different question (K-31) and must not be aggregated with project-grain figures.

evidence.detail: K-07 Contracted commitment has no connected source; declined

ask_answers.question: Which projects hold authorization but show no activity this year?
ask_answers.summary: None at portfolio level — 0 projects match. But 732 In Planning projects have no actuals at all, which is a different condition.

blocks.markdown:
Testing FY26 actuals = 0 where FY26 working budget > 0 returns **0 projects**. Every project carrying an FY26 budget in this data has recorded at least some FY26 cost.

That result deserves suspicion rather than comfort. A real portfolio of 4,500 projects almost always has a stalled tail, and its absence here is a property of the fixture, not a finding about Northline.

The adjacent condition is real and larger: **732 projects In Planning** hold **$16,104,068,000** of active plan and **zero** inception-to-date actuals. Those are not stalled — they have not started, and they carry no FY26 working budget, so they do not meet the test above.

**Zero-activity and no-data are different states and this answer keeps them apart.** The In Planning cohort reads zero because the general ledger has no rows for those projects — an absence. If a project were genuinely stalled the ledger would carry rows with a zero FY26 sum, which is a presence. Nothing in this portfolio is in that second state.

ask_answers.summary: Portfolio burn is 21.2% — the ratio of the sums. Lead Program runs at 38.8%, Federal PFAS at 13.2%.

The mean of the 4,193 individual project ratios is **21.6%** — close here, but the two are different measurements and only the first one answers this question. ask_answers.question: If spend continues at the current rate, where does the year land?
ask_answers.summary: A straight run-rate extrapolation lands FY26 at $10.57b — $815.3m below the Working Forecast.

blocks.markdown:
**This is an extrapolation, not a forecast.** Five months of actuals ($4,405,667,596 through May) annualise to **$10,573,602,229**. The planning system's own forecast — a different number with a different owner and a different method — says **$11,388,920,975**.

The extrapolation runs **$815,318,746 lower** because it assumes the first five months are representative. They are not: the Jan-calendarized budget phases 58.5% of the year into June–December, so a flat run-rate systematically understates a portfolio with a back-loaded construction season.

ask_answers.question: Where is forecast diverging from budget, by programme and category?
ask_answers.summary: Project-life forecast is $152.29b against an active plan of $113.08b — $39.22b above, concentrated in Plant large projects.

Both coordinates, stated: **Forecast (EAC) × Project life, latest** reads **$152,290,832,125**. **Approved budget × Project life, active** reads **$113,075,048,000**. The gap is **$39,215,784,125**, or 34.7% above the approved book.

ask_answers.question: What is the variance against the current approved baseline, and against the original?
ask_answers.summary: FY26 actuals are $590.7m under the phased budget. Against the original approved book the portfolio-life forecast is $39.22b over.

blocks.markdown:
Two readings from one materialised set, because the comparison is lost if you re-execute against a single baseline.

**Against the current approved baseline (year to date):** actuals $4,405,667,596 against phased budget $4,996,377,631 — **$-590,710,035**, -11.8%.

**Against the original approved baseline (project life):** the approval chain has moved the baseline on **2,426 projects**, up $1,141,966,000 and down $-671,415,000 — net $470,551,000. Measured against the *original* rather than the moved baseline, project-life forecast exposure is **$39,215,784,125**.

blocks.title: Baseline movement — up, down, net
blocks.note: Offsetting movements are shown separately; netting them hides that 2,426 baselines moved at all.

blocks.markdown: The distinction matters because a project sitting exactly on its current approved baseline can be materially over its original one — that population is HQ-11, and it is where trust in the reporting actually breaks.

ask_answers.question: How far has the approved baseline moved since original approval, and who approved each move?
ask_answers.summary: 2,426 of 4,500 projects have a moved baseline — net $470.6m. Approver identity is only available for the five contract-pack projects.

blocks.markdown:
**2,426 of 4,500 projects** carry a Most Recent Budget Plan that differs from their Active Budget Plan. Upward movement totals **$1,141,966,000**, downward **$-671,415,000**, net **$470,551,000**.

**On the second half of the question — who approved each move — the data is thin and this answer says so.** `northline_psoft.appr` carries a plan-version sequence and a status per version, which is enough to walk the chain. It does not carry an approving authority for every project. The graph holds **103 plan-version nodes** covering the five contract-pack projects and their peers; for the rest of the portfolio the chain exists as two values (active, most recent) with no named approver behind the move.

On Quarrydown the baseline moved from **$59,959,000** to **$61,158,000** — $1,199,000 — and seq 2 is *approved but not yet active*, so today's reporting still runs against seq 1. A reader quoting the active plan and a reader quoting the most recent plan will disagree by that amount and both will be right.

**Note the as-of.** `ds_psoft_appr` runs 7 days behind the other datasets, so the plan chain is the oldest contributing source in this answer. Any figure derived from it inherits that floor — see HQ-33.

ask_answers.question: What did the forecast add between the 3+9 and the 6+6 cut for this fiscal year?
ask_answers.summary: Cannot answer — the 6+6 round was never produced for FY26.

blocks.markdown:
The 6+6 forecast round does not exist for FY26. `FY26 Forecast 6+6` is present as a column and empty on all 4,500 projects; the same is true of 9+3. Only the **3+9** round ran, alongside the continuously-maintained **Working Forecast**.

**This is an absence, not a zero.** Reporting the movement as $12,021,894,758 — 3+9 minus a 6+6 of nothing — would state that the re-forecast removed the entire year, which is false. The correct answer is that one of the two operands does not exist.

**What I can compare instead**, if you want the movement question answered against cuts that do exist: 3+9 at $12,021,894,758 against the Working Forecast at $11,388,920,975 — a movement of $-632,973,783. Note that `working` is a **reserved selector**, not a member of the forecast cycle, so that is a comparison across two different kinds of thing and is labelled as such.

ask_answers.question: Which projects show no variance against current approved but material variance against original?
ask_answers.summary: 1,652 projects. $347.0m of variance was absorbed by baseline movement; $14.33b still sits above the moved baseline.

blocks.markdown:
**1,652 projects** have both had their baseline moved *and* still carry a material forecast gap against the moved baseline.

The baseline movement absorbed **$347,014,000** of variance on those projects — that is variance which no longer appears in any report run against the current approved figure. Above the moved baseline, **$14,334,876,657** is still exposed. Measured against the original approved book, total exposure on this cohort is **$14,681,890,657**.

**This is the question the domain actually asks**, and the answer names the movement rather than reporting a clean variance. A project whose baseline moved up by the same amount its forecast moved up reports zero variance and has consumed real capital.

ask_answers.question: How does the forward plan compare with the sum of project-life forecasts?
ask_answers.summary: The FY27–32 forward plan (MTP2026_v3) is $110.39b; the working budget over the same span is $116.25b — $5.86b higher.

blocks.markdown:
**Both spans stated.** The adopted forward plan is **MTP2026_v3** over **FY27–FY32**, totalling **$110,387,575,359**. The working budget across the same six years totals **$116,252,120,280**. The forward plan sits **$5,864,544,920** below the working view — 5.3%.

**The reconciliation does not close, and here is why it cannot.** A forward plan contains programme-level provisions for projects that do not exist yet as records, and it excludes project-level detail the working budget carries. The two are different objects measured over the same calendar, not two versions of one number. Anyone presenting the difference as a variance is asserting a reconciliation that the data does not support.

ask_answers.question: Which projects are trending to overrun, and by how much?
ask_answers.summary: 2,966 projects clear the materiality floor, carrying $26.87b. Ranked by the floor, not by magnitude.

blocks.markdown:
**The materiality policy first, because it determines the answer.** A project is admitted to this ranking when its forecast gap is **≥ $2,000,000** *and* **≥ 5% of its Most Recent Budget Plan**. Both conditions, not either.

Under that policy **2,966 projects** are trending to overrun, carrying **$26,871,563,138**. Without the floor the population is 3,688 projects and $27,619,449,607 — so the floor removes **722 projects and $747,886,469**, which is 2.7% of the gross figure and almost none of the decision.

A further **207 projects** carry no Most Recent Budget Plan at all. They have no baseline to overrun and are excluded from the population rather than ranked at zero.

blocks.title: Ranked by gap — top 15 over the materiality floor

blocks.markdown:
**Read the top of this list carefully.** The largest gaps by absolute value are Overhead projects, which are standing cost carriers rather than discrete builds — a project-life EAC against a project-life approval is a weak comparison for them. The first genuinely actionable rows are the Plant large projects and PFAS entries further down.

**On the portfolio-level bias.** 3,688 of 4,500 projects forecast above their baseline. A portfolio where four in five projects overrun is telling you something about the estimating basis rather than about delivery. Treat the ranking as relative, not as an absolute count of troubled projects.

ask_answers.question: Why did the estimate at completion move on Quarrydown WTP?
ask_answers.summary: Decomposition first: $15,618,600 of movement, of which $1,199,000 was absorbed by a baseline revision. No explanation is on record.

blocks.markdown:
**Decomposition before explanation.** On **C25B315_658** (C25B315_658-PFAS - Quarrydown WTP):

- Active Budget Plan: **$59,959,000**
- Most Recent Budget Plan: **$61,158,000** — the baseline moved up $1,199,000, approved but not yet active
- Forecast (EAC), project life: **$76,776,600**
- Gap above the moved baseline: **$15,618,600** (25.5%)

So the movement splits into a **$1,199,000** authorized revision and a **$15,618,600** unauthorized forecast increase.

**No explanation is attached to this movement.** The connected sources carry no annotation ledger, and the project's document set — the scope document in Drive — predates the revision. An explanation, if one exists, is in contractor correspondence that is not connected as a build-time source.

That is the honest state and it is not a failure of the decomposition. The decomposition above stands on its own; an attached explanation would sit beside it, never in place of it.

ask_answers.question: Which movements have an explanation on record, and which are unexplained?
ask_answers.summary: 0 of 2,966 obliged movements carry an explanation. There is no annotation ledger in the connected data.

blocks.markdown:
**Denominator first, and it is the obligation floor, not the signal floor.** 2,966 projects clear the materiality floor and are therefore obliged to carry an explanation. The signal floor — anything moving at all — would put 3,688 projects in the denominator and make the coverage figure look better by diluting it.

Explanation coverage is **0%**. No annotation ledger is connected. The four BigQuery datasets carry no free-text variance-reason column, and the Drive document set is scope and contract material rather than variance commentary.

blocks.title: Explanation coverage over the obligation floor
blocks.note: Coverage is computed over the obligation floor. Using the signal floor as the denominator would not change the numerator and would only move the percentage.

blocks.markdown: **What would change this.** Contractor correspondence is where variance reasons actually live in this business, and Gmail is available as a *runtime* source — it produces observations that resolve against the graph at query time. Runtime observations are not graph elements and do not become an annotation ledger; a ledger is a build-time artifact someone has to author. Connecting mail improves the answer to HQ-19, not to this one.

ask_answers.question: Is this overrun scope, escalation, schedule, or estimate error?
ask_answers.summary: Cannot categorize from the connected data. The only evidenced driver categories in the package are the 22 change-order bases in the contract documents.

blocks.markdown:
**Categories must be evidenced, not inferred from the shape of the movement.** Nothing in the four BigQuery datasets carries a variance-driver classification, so for 2,966 of the 2,966 material overruns the honest answer is *unclassified*.

The one place evidenced categories exist is the contract document set. **22 change orders** across the five contract-pack projects carry a stated basis in their own text — differing site conditions, owner-directed scope addition, schedule extension, and so on. **'On track' is a position, not a verdict.** The graph reports where each project sits relative to a date somebody configured. It does not judge whether the programme will meet the rule — that requires an assessment of what the rule actually requires at each system, which is a regulatory judgement and not a query result.

**Peak delivery is 2030**, one year past the configured entry: 110 projects worth $4,174,638,967.

ask_answers.question: Are we replacing lead service lines fast enough to meet the mandated rate?
ask_answers.summary: **The replacement rate is not computable from connected data.** A mandated rate is lines per year against a known inventory; this package has projects and budget, and no service-line inventory at all.

blocks.markdown: **What the question needs, and what exists:**

blocks.title: Inputs required for a replacement rate
rows: Total service lines in the system
GL carries dollars, not line counts

blocks.markdown:
**The unknown-material trap.** Under LCRI a line of unknown material is treated as lead until proven otherwise, and inventory work reclassifies large numbers of them without replacing a single pipe. A dashboard that counts reclassifications as progress reports a replacement rate that is mostly paperwork. **An unknown-material line that becomes a known copper line is not a replaced line.** Any rate this platform eventually reports must state inventory completeness beside it, or the rate is uninterpretable.

**What can be said today.** 443 projects sit in the Lead Program with $9,857,465,339 of working budget, 28.3% of it spent. All 342 that carry a planned in-service date land in 2026. That is a spend position, and it is not a replacement rate — the two are related only by an assumed cost per line that nobody has supplied.

**What connecting a source would change.** A service-line inventory (typically GIS or the customer system) makes the numerator and denominator real. Until then this question has an honest partial answer and no complete one.
**Do not derive lines from dollars.** $2,791,392,661 divided by an assumed unit cost would produce a line count precise to four digits and grounded in nothing. The refusal is the answer.

document.heading: What-if
document.subtitle: Stress the remaining forecast to complete without pretending to predict it. A what-if moves one attributable driver at a time — index-linked materials, labor, contingency — and recomputes only the slice the graph can tie to that driver. What it can't attribute is shown as a locked residual, not smeared across the answer. Nothing is forecast; every slice opens to its source. Authoring sets the scenario — which measures you watch, which drivers a case may move and how far, and its name. Runtime is where you move the sliders across cases, publish the complete scenario when it is worth sharing, and open any figure to the contract, timesheet or index feed it came from.
